newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: INTERVIEW - Tata Tea bullish on Sri Lanka.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Tata Tea bullish on Sri Lanka.

text.p: India's largest tea firm, Tata Tea Ltd, which acquired a controlling stake in a Sri Lankan plantation last year, will look at other Sri Lankan acquisitions, the firm's managing director said on Friday.
R.K. Krishna Kumar said Tata also planned to expand into other tea-producing countries soon.
"Both in tea and coffee, Tata Tea has drawn up plans for large-scale global expansion," he told Reuters. "Our move into Sri Lanka is part of that plan."

He said Tata Tea, a member of the Tata Group, India's largest industrial group, had plans to acquire tea gardens in Kenya, Uganda, Zambia, Tanzania and Georgia in the Commonwealth of Independent States.
The acquisitions would make Tata Tea the only company in the world with production bases in all three major tea-producing belts -- India, Sri Lanka and East Africa, he added.
"We would like to have a viable and strong presence in any area of the world where tea is grown," Krishna Kumar said.

Tata Tea, which has 55 estates spread over 26,000 hectares in the Indian states of Assam, West Bangal, Kerala and Tamil Nadu, made its overseas debut in 1992 when it took over the management of Sri Lanka's Kahawatte Plantations under a government plan to privatise management of 23 plantation firms.
In February 1996 the company acquired 51 percent of Watawala Plantations Ltd for 316 million rupees ($5.4 million), after the government began privatising ownership of plantations.

Tata Tea bought Watawala through local firm Estate Management Services Pvt Ltd (EMSPL), keeping in line with Sri Lanka's privatisation policy which prevents foreign ownership of more than 49 percent of the equity of an estate firm.
Tata Tea holds 49 percent of EMSPL's equity.
Watawala Plantations has 20 estates with a total area of 12,435 hectares. Of these, 15 are tea estates spread over 5,126 hectares while three are tea-cum-rubber estates.
"We are now consolidating our investment in Watawala. We are concentrating on improving field conditions, filling, replanting, soil conservation and employee welfare," Krishna Kumar said.
The company is currently investing about 90 million rupees ($1.5 million) on the improvements, he said.
By the end of this year, Watawala would be exporting 40 percent of its annual production of 10 million kg in value-added form, company officials said.
"In Sri Lanka, the infrastructure for value addition (to tea) is superb. We want to make good use of that," Krishna Kumar said.
He said after nearly five years of involvement in the Sri Lankan tea industry, Tata Tea remained bullish about the local industry.

"There are more plantation companies coming up on offer. We would like to look at some of these opportunities and see if we can play a role either in acquiring more companies or in participating in their management," he said.

Sri Lanka has completed privatising six firms, which are now trading on the Colombo Stock Exchange. The first step of selling 51 percent to a strategic investor has been completed in seven more, including Watawala. Privatisation of the remaining 10 is expected to begin shortly.
Sri Lanka, the world's second-largest tea exporter, produced a record high 258.4 million kg in calendar 1996. Of this, it exported 244 million kg.
